description: DEF CON 33 Creator Stage showcases technical presentations, hardware demonstrations, and research by independent security creators, builders, and practitioners. Talks cover embedded hardware exploitation, automotive and aerospace security, maritime systems, industrial control networks, vulnerability disclosure, and applied machine learning.

talks.title: Hacker v. Triage - Inside Bug Bounty Battleground
talks.teaser: Examines friction between security researchers and vulnerability triagers, offering actionable strategies to resolve severity disputes and improve collaboration.
talks.summary:
Bug Bounty Battlegrounds and Triage Dynamics

Bug bounty programs often operate as tense environments where security researchers and vulnerability triagers disagree over bug validity, severity ratings, and reward payouts. This friction can strain professional relationships, yet it also presents an opportunity for collaboration and community building when approached constructively.

Real-World Conflict Scenarios

Common flashpoints include severity rating debates over subtle behaviors like Gmail aliasing, unclear report submissions, and controversial gray-area vulnerability rejections such as business logic flaws. Researchers and triage teams also encounter complex escalations involving disputed CVE assignments.

Communication and Business Impact Framing

Bridging the divide between researchers and triagers requires clear communication and business impact framing. Researchers improve outcomes by articulating precise exploit scenarios and potential business damage rather than relying on abstract severity calculators.

Strategic Value Beyond Bounties

Beyond immediate payouts, bug bounty engagements offer researchers a pathway to build professional networks, enhance personal branding, and advance security careers through professional collaboration and high-quality reporting.

talks.title: Go Malware Meets IoT: Challenges, Blind Spots, and Botnets
talks.teaser: Examines the challenges of analyzing Go-based IoT malware and demonstrates reversing techniques using the Pumabot surveillance botnet as a case study.
talks.summary:
The Rise of Go in IoT Malware

Go-based malware is increasingly prevalent in IoT environments due to the language's cross-compilation support and architectural flexibility. However, these same attributes complicate analysis and defense, as Go binaries are large, statically compiled, and structured differently from traditional C-based binaries.

Reversing Challenges in Go Binaries

Analysts encounter significant obstacles when analyzing Go runtimes, including complex type systems, non-standard function call conventions, and obscured string tables. Traditional static analysis tools struggle to extract meaningful strings or recover function boundaries without specialized tooling.

Practical Recovery and Analysis Techniques

Decompilation and reverse engineering workflows benefit from dedicated scripts and plugins designed to parse Go internal metadata structures, reconstruct type definitions, and restore original symbol names from stripped binaries.

Case Study: Pumabot Botnet

Pumabot represents a real-world example of Go-based malware targeting IoT surveillance devices and IP cameras. Analyzing Pumabot reveals its infection vectors, persistence mechanisms, command-and-control communication protocols, and the distinctive forensic artifacts left on compromised endpoints.

talks.title: From Pwn to Plan: Turning Physical Exploits Into Upgrades
talks.teaser: Walks through the full physical penetration testing lifecycle, from breach-focused reconnaissance to delivering actionable security upgrades for clients.
talks.summary:
The Complete Physical Assessment Lifecycle

Physical penetration testing involves far more than just gaining unauthorized entry into a building. Effective assessments balance tactical execution with safety, compliance, and actionable remediation that delivers real organizational value.

Reconnaissance and Breach-Focused OSINT

Successful physical engagements begin with thorough open-source intelligence and onsite reconnaissance. Operators analyze facility layouts, employee routines, badge types, and entry points to identify viable physical access pathways before attempting access.

Executing Controlled Physical Breaches

Physical entry operations must follow strict rules of engagement to avoid safety hazards or operational disruptions. Real-world testing tests access control doors, egress hardware, and human-layer security under controlled conditions.

Translating Exploits into Defensive Upgrades

The true value of physical red teaming lies in transforming break-in findings into meaningful defensive upgrades. Reports must provide clear architectural and procedural recommendations that facility managers and security teams can immediately implement.

talks.title: The Anatomy of a Crypto Scam
talks.teaser: Breaks down operational workflows and financial mechanics of cryptocurrency fraud, tracking stolen funds and detailing defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Deconstructing Modern Cryptocurrency Fraud

Cryptocurrency scams have evolved into highly organized fraudulent operations that exploit human psychology and financial deception. Researchers observe and interact with active scam operations to map out their technical infrastructure and operational tradecraft.

Workflow and Deception Mechanics

Scammers deploy multi-stage social engineering schemes to convince victims to transfer digital assets to attacker-controlled wallets. Deceptive workflows often simulate fake investment platforms, remote desktop access, or fraudulent customer support interactions.

Tracking Illicit Fund Flows

Following on-chain transactions reveals how criminal actors move stolen funds through intermediary wallets, decentralized exchanges, and mixing services to obfuscate transaction trails before cash-out.

Defensive Strategies and Countermeasures

Mitigating crypto scams requires a combination of user education, exchange-level fraud monitoring, and automated transaction risk scoring to detect and block suspicious transfers before funds are permanently lost.

talks.title: Regex For Hackers
talks.teaser: Demonstrates practical regular expression techniques for bug bounty hunters to uncover hidden API endpoints, bypass filters, and extract secrets from code repositories.
talks.summary:
Practical Regex Tradecraft for Security Researchers

Automated vulnerability scanners often miss nuanced security flaws and hidden endpoints that manual analysis with tailored regular expressions can readily uncover. Mastering regex patterns allows researchers to accelerate recon and target high-value assets effectively.

Bypassing Filters and Validations

Security controls like postMessage origins and CORS validation routines frequently contain flawed regular expressions. Subtle flaws in pattern boundaries, unescaped characters, or weak regex anchors allow attackers to bypass intended origin restrictions.

Uncovering Hidden API Endpoints and Secrets

Analyzing client-side JavaScript bundles and GitHub repositories with targeted regex patterns extracts sensitive endpoints, hidden routes, and embedded API keys. Crafting precise search queries cuts through minified code to identify undocumented functionality.

Exploiting Application Logic and Redirects

Understanding parser behavior enables researchers to transform seemingly benign open redirects into full account takeovers and spot Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attack vectors that automated tools overlook.

talks.title: Intro to Physical Security Bypass
talks.teaser: Explores non-destructive entry techniques that bypass doors and access control hardware without picking locks, alongside defensive hardening measures.
talks.summary:
Foundations of Physical Security Bypass

Physical security assessments often bypass doors without manipulating lock cylinders directly. Access control hardware, egress mechanisms, and door framing frequently contain mechanical vulnerabilities that allow rapid entry.

Common Egress and Latch Bypass Vectors

Latch slip tools, under-door tools, and request-to-exit sensor manipulation allow attackers to open secured doors by exploiting gaps in door sweeps, framing, or hardware installation. Poorly shielded crash bars and sensor blind spots provide immediate bypass pathways.

Access Control Weaknesses

Improperly installed magnetic locks, electric strikes, and power supplies introduce points of failure. Failure to supervise request-to-exit wiring or protect request-to-exit sensors allows physical triggers to release locking mechanisms unhindered.

Defensive Hardening Recommendations

Hardening facilities requires installing latch guards, full-length astragals, shielded request-to-exit sensors, and properly aligned door closers to eliminate mechanical bypass vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Managing Bug Bounties @ Scale
talks.teaser: Leaders from major enterprise bug bounty programs discuss triage operations, researcher relationships, reward structures, and scaling challenges.
talks.summary:
Scaling Enterprise Bug Bounty Operations

Managing enterprise-scale bug bounty programs requires balancing high report volumes with efficient triage workflows and engineering remediation pipelines. Program managers from large technology organizations must structure programs to attract skilled researchers while minimizing noise.

Triage and Researcher Engagement

Maintaining positive relationships with researchers hinges on clear communication, prompt triage responses, and consistent reward expectations. Transparent bounty guidelines and constructive feedback prevent disputes and encourage long-term researcher engagement.

Reward Structures and Budgeting

Structuring bounty rewards involves aligning payouts with realistic business risk and exploit impact. Competitive payout tiers incentivize researchers to investigate complex business logic and architectural flaws rather than flooding programs with low-severity scanner outputs.

Internal Alignment and Program Evolution

Building internal buy-in across engineering and executive leadership ensures that identified vulnerabilities are prioritized and patched swiftly. Modern bug bounty programs continually adapt their scopes and rules of engagement to reflect evolving cloud and application architectures.

talks.title: Designing and Participating in AI Bug Bounty Programs
talks.teaser: Deep dives into adversarial prompt injection, context poisoning, and RAG manipulation flaws to help researchers find and demonstrate high-impact AI vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
The Emerging AI Vulnerability Landscape

Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) into applications introduces novel vulnerability classes that bypass traditional web defenses. Understanding how AI models process context and instructions is essential for uncovering high-impact flaws.

Adversarial Prompting and Indirect Prompt Injection

Attackers craft indirect prompt injection payloads embedded within external data sources, web pages, or documents. When an AI agent ingests this untrusted content, the embedded prompt hijacks the model's instruction flow to execute unauthorized actions or exfiltrate private data.

Context Poisoning and RAG Manipulation

Retrieval pipelines can be manipulated by injecting malicious documents into vector knowledge bases. By poisoning indexed context, attackers alter model reasoning, force incorrect data retrieval, and trigger unauthorized API executions.

Demonstrating Business Impact in Bug Bounties

Successfully reporting AI vulnerabilities requires researchers to articulate clear exploit chains and business consequences. Documenting reproducible multi-step prompt injection chains helps organizations understand severity and implement robust guardrails.

talks.title: No Brain No Gain
talks.teaser: Proposes using unique dynamic brain electrical activity from EEG signals as a lightweight authentication layer resilient against deepfake spoofing in IoT devices.
talks.summary:
Biometric Authentication Challenges in IoT

Constrained IoT devices struggle to support heavy cryptographic computation while facing sophisticated human-layer and sensor-spoofing attacks. Static biometric identifiers, such as fingerprints and facial scans, are increasingly susceptible to deepfakes and physical replication.

Dynamic Neural Authentication via EEG

Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals capture unique, dynamic electrical activity produced by the brain. Because neural firing patterns vary across individuals and change dynamically, EEG signals provide an authentication modality that is inherently resistant to static replay and spoofing.

Lightweight Architecture for Constrained Devices

Processing neural signals on low-power IoT hardware requires lightweight feature extraction algorithms. By extracting distinct frequency bands and temporal characteristics without heavy machine learning models, devices achieve secure verification within tight compute constraints.

Security and Privacy Implications

Grounding device trust in biological neural patterns eliminates the need to store sensitive raw biometric templates, providing resilient, privacy-preserving authentication for smart environments.

talks.title: How Not to IoT: Lessons in Security Failures
talks.teaser: Surveys pervasive architectural and implementation failures in consumer IoT gadgets, highlighting cleartext credentials, command injections, and insecure defaults.
talks.summary:
Common Architectural Flaws in Consumer IoT

Consumer IoT devices frequently exhibit fundamental security shortcomings due to rushed development cycles and cost constraints. Critical vulnerabilities often stem from basic design flaws rather than complex memory corruption bugs.

Cleartext Communication and Insecure Pairing

Many smart devices transmit sensitive data, including home Wi-Fi credentials and administrative passwords, over unencrypted HTTP connections during setup and operation. Insecure pairing protocols expose local network secrets to passive eavesdroppers.

Command Injection and Hardcoded Secrets

Web management interfaces and CGI binaries on routers and network-attached storage (NAS) devices frequently suffer from unauthenticated command injection vulnerabilities. Static, vendor-wide encryption keys embedded in firmware further compromise alarm systems and smart peripherals.

Firmware and System-Level Weaknesses

Reliance on outdated BusyBox utilities, obsolete Linux kernels, and pre-installed malware in off-brand Android gadgets creates persistent attack surfaces. Addressing these widespread issues requires secure firmware baselines and rigorous automated validation.

talks.title: All your keyboards are belong to us!
talks.teaser: Tutorial on keyboard attack vectors, ranging from hardware keyloggers and Van Eck phreaking electromagnetic emanations to acoustic typing eavesdropping.
talks.summary:
Keyboard Attack Vectors and Data Interception

Attacking keyboards allows adversaries to capture plaintext credentials and confidential input before cryptographic encryption takes place. Intercepting keystrokes at the physical interface bypasses complex network and application security controls.

Hardware Keylogging and Inline Interceptors

Physical keyloggers installed between the keyboard cable and computer port log raw keystroke scancodes to non-volatile memory. Modern inline hardware implants leverage wireless transmitters or cellular modems for remote keystroke exfiltration.

Electromagnetic Emanations and Van Eck Phreaking

Unshielded keyboard cables and internal microcontroller traces emit subtle electromagnetic radiation during typing. By tuning software-defined radios to these unintended emanations, attackers can reconstruct keystrokes from meters away without physical contact.

Acoustic Eavesdropping and Side-Channel Analysis

Differences in key acoustics allow machine learning models trained on audio recordings to identify individual keystrokes based on typing sound signatures. Defending against keyboard side-channel attacks requires physical inspection, shielded hardware, and acoustic noise generation.

talks.title: Threat Dynamics on the Seas
talks.teaser: National security experts explore maritime cybersecurity threats, from port crane operations and naval systems to the geopolitical vulnerability of undersea cables.
talks.summary:
Geopolitical and Cybersecurity Dynamics at Sea

The maritime domain serves as a vital artery for global commerce, power projection, and digital communications. As maritime operations digitize, ports, commercial shipping, and naval forces face escalating cyber threats from nation-states and criminal actors.

Vulnerabilities in Port Infrastructure

Modern container terminals rely on automated cargo handling equipment, ship-to-shore cranes, and terminal operating systems. Compromising these networked operational technology systems can disrupt supply chains and stall economic throughput across major shipping hubs.

Undersea Cables and Communication Resilience

Undersea fiber-optic cables carry the overwhelming majority of international internet traffic. Threats ranging from physical sabotage to electronic interception pose profound risks to global connectivity and national security communications.

Strategic Defense and International Governance

Securing the maritime theater requires coordinated defense strategies between naval authorities, commercial operators, and international allies to monitor threats, safeguard physical subsea cables, and defend critical maritime IT/OT networks.

talks.title: SSH-nanigans: Busting Open the Mainframes Iron Fortress Through Unix
talks.teaser: Demonstrates practical attack paths against IBM z/OS Unix System Services, showing how weak file permissions and buffer overflows allow privilege escalation on mainframes.
talks.summary:
The Overlooked Unix Side of IBM z/OS

While mainframe penetration testing traditionally focuses on MVS and ISPF interfaces, IBM z/OS includes a complete Unix environment known as Unix System Services (OMVS). This environment exposes distinct attack paths that enterprise defenders often neglect.

File Hygiene and Database Exposure

Inadequate file system permissions in OMVS frequently expose sensitive configuration files, database credentials, and unencrypted dataset backups. Attackers leveraging standard Unix shells can discover credentials that facilitate lateral movement into mainframe databases.

Privilege Escalation via APF Authorized Datasets

Misconfigured External Security Manager (ESM) rules and poorly restricted superuser permissions allow attackers to execute privileged commands. Demonstrating buffer overflows in Authorized Program Facility (APF) datasets illustrates how local shell access leads to complete control.

Detection and Defensive Hardening

Securing z/OS Unix environments requires enforcing strict dataset protection, auditing OMVS superuser privileges, and deploying monitoring tools to detect anomalous Unix commands on mainframe infrastructure.

talks.title: How NOT to Perform Covert Entry Assessments
talks.teaser: Shares hard-learned lessons and busted myths from physical penetration tests, covering site surveys, social engineering, and real-time contingency handling.
talks.summary:
Realities of Covert Entry Operations

Covert physical entry assessments require meticulous planning, calm decision-making, and disciplined operational tradecraft. Relying on cinematic tropes or aggressive improvisations frequently leads to compromised engagements and safety hazards.

Physical Site Surveys and Reconnaissance

Effective assessments begin with discreet reconnaissance of physical security perimeters, camera coverage, guard rotations, and electronic badge readers. Rushing into an engagement without thorough surveillance increases the likelihood of premature detection.

Human-Layer Social Engineering and Pretexting

Face-to-face social engineering requires credible pretexting tailored to the target facility. Operators must manage interpersonal interactions smoothly, avoiding high-friction confrontations that trigger security escalations.

Troubleshooting When Operations Go Sideways

When unexpected challenges occur—such as encountering altered floor plans, malfunctioning bypass tools, or curious employees—operators must rely on established fallback protocols and de-escalation strategies to maintain safety and compliance.

talks.title: Flipping Locks: Remote Badge Cloning with the Flipper Zero and More
talks.teaser: Details custom hardware designs and social engineering tactics to remotely clone RFID access badges from a distance, including HID iClass SE downgrade attacks.
talks.summary:
Limitations of Traditional RFID Badge Cloning

Standard RFID badge cloning typically requires close physical proximity (under three feet) to a target individual. In modern hybrid work environments with reduced office foot traffic, close-range cloning becomes logistically difficult for physical red teams.

Long-Range and Standalone Hardware Implants

Custom hardware implants—such as high-gain gooseneck readers, hidden wall devices, and modified clipboards—allow operators to capture RFID credential data at extended distances without direct physical interaction with targets.

HID iClass Downgrade and Legacy Attacks

Many physical access control systems configured for HID iClass SE or SEOS maintain backwards compatibility with legacy credential formats. Operators exploit these compatibility modes to execute downgrade attacks that capture cloneable legacy badge identifiers.

Countermeasures for Facility Defense

Hardening access control perimeters requires disabling legacy credential compatibility on badge readers, deploying encrypted OSDP wiring, and monitoring reader tamper alerts to detect unauthorized hardware implants.

talks.title: Hacking Hotel Locks: The Saflok Vulnerabilities Expanded
talks.teaser: Expands on Saflok hotel electronic lock vulnerabilities, detailing weaknesses in the handheld programmer interface, bit fields, and unencrypted credential data.
talks.summary:
Architecture of Offline Hotel Access Systems

Saflok electronic door locks are deployed across thousands of hotels and apartment complexes throughout North America. These locks operate using offline authentication mechanisms that rely on stored cryptographic state and pre-programmed credentials.

Analyzing the Handheld Programmer Interface

Interrogating the proprietary handheld programmer and lock programming interface reveals security weaknesses in device initialization and lock provisioning. Attackers can extract configuration data and manipulate lock parameters without administrative authorization.

Bit Fields and Unencrypted Credential Data

Deconstructing RFID keycard data structures exposes unencrypted bit fields and weak cryptographic checksums. Understanding these data formats allows researchers to craft custom master credentials that unlock target doors throughout a facility.

Mitigation and Security Architecture Lessons

Addressing offline lock vulnerabilities requires deploying updated lock firmware, transitioning to encrypted online management systems, and eliminating reliance on security-through-obscurity in access control hardware.

talks.title: State of Open Source in the Federal Government
talks.teaser: Discusses the adoption, governance, and policy landscape of open-source software within US federal agencies and defense departments.
talks.summary:
In this presentation on the DEF CON 33 Creator Stage, an advocate for public technology delivers an assessment of the current state of open-source software (OSS) across United States federal agencies. Opening at 00:00, the speaker discusses how adopting and contributing to open source enhances federal technological agility, transparency, and cybersecurity posture.

At 07:00, the talk evaluates the economic and security benefits of open source in government, explaining how public code sharing reduces taxpayer waste, accelerates feature deployment, and enables crowd-sourced vulnerability identification. At 14:00, the speaker examines federal policy frameworks, notably OMB Memorandum M-16-21 and its pilot requirement for federal agencies to release a minimum of 20% of custom-developed software as open source.

Highlighting successful implementations at 21:00, the presenter spotlights the U.S. Web Design System (USWDS) developed by the General Services Administration (GSA). Concluding at 28:00, the speaker outlines actionable goals for expanding federal OSS publication, establishing agency open source program offices (OSPOs), and welcoming external community contributions to public repositories. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Quantum Resistant Healthcare
talks.teaser: Examines the impending quantum computing threat to healthcare infrastructure and outlines Siemens Healthineers' strategies for migrating to post-quantum cryptography.
talks.summary:
The Quantum Threat to Healthcare Infrastructure

Advances in quantum computing pose a systemic threat to public-key cryptography used across the healthcare sector. Algorithms securing electronic health records, connected medical devices, and telemedicine communications face obsolescence once cryptographically relevant quantum computers emerge.

Long-Term Data Protection and Eavesdropping

Healthcare data is subject to 'harvest now, decrypt later' threats, where encrypted medical communications and sensitive patient histories are intercepted today for future decryption once quantum decryption capabilities mature.

Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration at Scale

Siemens Healthineers and healthcare device vendors are planning transitions to NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. Upgrading legacy embedded medical hardware requires evaluating computational overhead, memory constraints, and certificate sizes.

Strategic Considerations for Critical Infrastructure

Securing medical environments demands proactive cryptographic inventory management, hybrid key-exchange deployments, and backward-compatible firmware update mechanisms to ensure long-term clinical safety.

talks.title: Elevators 101
talks.teaser: Explains how elevator floor lockouts function and how improperly configured elevator controllers and hoistways can be bypassed to access restricted floors.
talks.summary:
Elevator Systems in Physical Access Architecture

Elevators are frequently integrated into facility security architectures to enforce floor lockouts and restrict access to sensitive levels. However, misconfigurations and default operating states often undermine these intended physical boundaries.

Operating Modes and Controller Manipulation

Elevator controllers support specialized operational modes, such as independent service, fire recall, and maintenance states. Physical penetration testers can leverage physical key switches, controller interfaces, or signal bridging to activate these modes and bypass floor access restrictions.

Hoistway Entry and Traveling Cable Vulnerabilities

Accessing elevator hoistways, car tops, and traveling cable junctions exposes unencrypted signaling wiring. Tampering with controller relays or sensor inputs allows unauthorized transit between floors without authenticating through card readers.

Defensive Architecture and Hardening

Properly securing elevator installations requires supervising key-switch wiring, isolating maintenance mode inputs, and validating floor requests directly through integrated building access management systems.

talks.title: Dark Capabilities: When Tech Companies Go Offensive
talks.teaser: Explores the structural, offensive technical capabilities inherent in modern tech platforms and the risks posed when companies, insiders, or nation-states weaponize them.
talks.summary:
The Latent Power of Modern Tech Platforms

Global technology companies operate cloud infrastructures, mobile operating systems, and connected consumer hardware with pervasive administrative capabilities. Beyond their intended commercial functions, these platforms possess immense structural power to conduct targeted surveillance and digital operations.

Examples of Platform Reach and Data Access

Real-world glimpses illustrate this capability: cloud providers scanning private customer storage, rideshare platforms tracking user location beyond active rides, robotic vacuums mapping internal home layouts, and endpoint agents deploying software updates globally within minutes.

Weaponization by Insiders and Adversaries

The architectural access built into centralized technology platforms represents an attractive target for malicious insiders, coerced employees, and advanced state-sponsored threat actors seeking widespread access without developing traditional zero-day exploits.

Policy, Governance, and Platform Accountability

Mitigating systemic risks from tech platform power requires robust technical oversight, independent auditing, decentralized trust architectures, and regulatory frameworks governing administrative data access.

talks.title: Third Party Access Granted: Postmortem on Student Privacy
talks.teaser: Examines student data pipelines, third-party vendor integrations, consent frameworks, and privacy challenges across enterprise university systems.
talks.summary:
A student privacy researcher and advocate presents a critical postmortem on student data privacy on the Creator Stage, examining how legal exemptions and digital learning platforms expose student records to commercial entities [06:18, 12:13]. The speaker critiques broad institutional definitions of "directory information" under FERPA, explaining how loosely regulated classifications allow colleges to share sensitive student records without explicit consent.

The talk reveals how educational institutions routinely transmit bulk student data to external third parties, including the National Student Clearinghouse, financial aid vendors, and commercial predictive analytics services [18:00]. The speaker explains how aggregated academic histories and enrollment data are used to generate predictive algorithms and retention scores [23:45], highlighting the ethical hazards of non-consensual profiling. The session calls on students and faculty to demand transparency through mandatory disclosures of institutional data-sharing contracts and enforceable student opt-out rights [29:48].

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Building Onramps for Emergency Web Archiving in Ukraine and Beyond
talks.teaser: Highlights community-driven emergency web archiving efforts by Saving Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Online (SUCHO) to preserve cultural data during crisis.
talks.summary:
Web Application and API Security

This talk addresses web application vulnerabilities and exploitation techniques. Topics include injection attacks, cross-site scripting, authentication bypasses, API security, and modern web framework vulnerabilities.

(AI summary — Claude Haiku)

talks.title: Fighting a Digital Blockade: View from Taiwan
talks.teaser: Taiwanese digital affairs officials and experts discuss digital blockade scenarios, undersea infrastructure protection, and cyber-resilience against nation-state threats.
talks.summary:
The Threat of Digital Blockades

Island nations and isolated territories face unique cybersecurity risks from potential digital blockades, where adversaries combine physical sabotage of communications infrastructure with large-scale cyber disruptions to sever external connectivity.

Undersea Cable Vulnerabilities and Sabotage

Undersea fiber-optic cables represent critical chokepoints for international data traffic. Physical tampering, anchor-dragging incidents, and coordinated subsea disruptions threaten to isolate national communication networks during geopolitical conflicts.

National Cyber Resilience Strategies

Defending against digital blockades requires building multi-layered communication redundancy, incorporating low Earth orbit satellite constellations, decentralized domestic routing, and hardened emergency backup networks.

International Coordination and Policy Frameworks

Securing subsea infrastructure demands cross-border partnerships, shared maritime threat intelligence, and international legal frameworks to deter and respond to attacks on critical communication arteries.

talks.title: Satellite Networks Under Siege: Cybersecurity Challenges of Targeted DDoS
talks.teaser: Investigates low Earth orbit satellite constellation vulnerabilities to targeted DDoS attacks using dynamic topology modeling and the HYDRA botnet framework.
talks.summary:
Cybersecurity Dynamics in Low Earth Orbit

The proliferation of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations for global broadband connectivity introduces complex cybersecurity challenges. Dynamic network topologies, inter-satellite laser links, and constrained orbital resources create unique vulnerabilities absent in terrestrial networks.

Targeted DDoS in Orbital Networks

Adversaries exploit predictable orbital mechanics and cross-satellite routing constraints to launch highly disruptive Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. Because bandwidth on inter-satellite links and ground station downlinks is finite, even modest botnet volumes can induce cascading routing failures.

The HYDRA Multi-Zone Botnet Framework

Research using the HYDRA framework demonstrates how coordinated botnets can strategically distribute attack traffic across multiple ground gateway zones. Optimizing traffic injection based on orbital visibility maximizes communication disruption while minimizing the attacker's required footprint.

Defensive Architecture and Traffic Engineering

Securing space-based broadband networks requires dynamic orbital traffic rerouting, rate-limiting at ground ingress gateways, and decentralized anomaly detection across spaceborne routing payloads.

talks.title: The Worst ICS OT Love Story Ever Told
talks.teaser: Traces the convergence between state adversaries, ransomware cartels, and hacktivists targeting industrial control systems and operational technology.
talks.summary:
Evolution of Industrial Control Threats

Securing operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) has undergone fundamental transformations over the past decade. Historically focused on defending against sophisticated nation-state actors, industrial defenders now face a rapidly diversifying adversary landscape.

The Post-Colonial Pipeline Threat Shift

Following high-profile disruptions like the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack, criminal ransomware cartels and politically motivated hacktivists turned their focus toward critical infrastructure, demonstrating that operational disruptions could be achieved without bespoke ICS malware.

Convergence of State, Criminal, and Hacktivist Actors

Modern threat dynamics reflect increasing alignment and tool-sharing between state-sponsored groups, ransomware gangs, and hacktivist collectives. Advanced exploitation tooling and modular attack frameworks are now deployed by adversaries possessing varied skill levels.

Defensive Preparation and Infrastructure Hardening

Securing industrial facilities requires moving beyond perimeter firewalls by enforcing zero-trust OT network segmentation, monitoring east-west industrial protocols, and developing robust incident response playbooks for physical operational environments.

talks.title: State of the Pops: Mapping the Digital Waters
talks.teaser: Presents findings from passive OSINT reconnaissance across the top 50 global maritime organizations, analyzing DNS, email authentication, and exposed services.
talks.summary:
Passive Reconnaissance in the Maritime Industry

As global maritime shipping digitizes, the cybersecurity posture of foundational internet infrastructure across maritime enterprises remains uneven. Evaluating this posture through passive, non-intrusive open-source intelligence (OSINT) surfaces critical visibility into sector-wide vulnerabilities.

Methodology: Mapping Top 50 Maritime Organizations

A large-scale OSINT assessment evaluated the public digital footprints of the top 50 maritime shipping and logistics organizations. The research relied entirely on public records, DNS registries, and passive telemetry without transmitting intrusive network packets to target systems.

Findings in DNS and Email Security Protocols

Analysis revealed widespread gaps in fundamental security controls, including missing or misconfigured SPF, DKIM, and DMARC email authentication records, unmanaged subdomains, and exposed administrative web interfaces.

Open-Source Tooling and Sector Resilience

Releasing the assessment methodology and analysis scripts empowers practitioners and asset owners to audit maritime infrastructure, benchmark organizational defenses, and strengthen foundational cyber hygiene across supply chain operations.

talks.title: China's Health Sector Ambitions and Info Needs
talks.teaser: Analyzes Chinese state-sponsored intelligence requirements and strategic cyber operations targeting the global healthcare and biotechnology sectors.
talks.summary:
This DEF CON talk covers china's health sector ambitions and info needs.

(AI summary — Claude Haiku)

talks.title: Pirates of the North Sea
talks.teaser: Details undercover maritime red team operations where testers boarded cruise ships to physically breach engine rooms, navigation bridges, and vessel IT networks.
talks.summary:
Undercover Red Teaming on Commercial Vessels

Maritime physical and logical security assessments evaluate how effectively commercial vessels and shipping companies protect onboard operational technology. In real-world engagements, red teamers board active passenger cruise ships disguised as regular guests to test physical boundaries.

Infiltrating Restricted Vessel Compartments

By exploiting social engineering opportunities and unlatched service corridors, operators successfully gained physical access to restricted zones, including ship communication centers and engine control rooms, while blending into crew and passenger traffic.

Bridging Physical Access to Vessel Operational Networks

Once inside control compartments, testers connected directly to shipboard network switches, bridging isolated passenger networks to critical operational buses. Vulnerabilities in maritime network segregation allowed testers to access navigation and propulsion systems.

Lessons for Maritime Fleet Security

Securing marine vessels requires enforcing electronic access controls on all crewways, hardening bridge network drops, and training crew members on physical tailgating and guest verification protocols.

talks.title: What’s Really in the Box? The Case for Hardware Provenance and HBOMs
talks.teaser: Makes the case for Hardware Bills of Materials (HBOMs) to trace semiconductor provenance, detect component cloning, and secure hardware supply chains.
talks.summary:
The Blind Spot in Hardware Supply Chains

While Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) have gained significant traction for software transparency, hardware component provenance remains an opaque black box. Counterfeit chips, unauthorized silicon revisions, and obscure fabrication origins create systemic security risks across critical infrastructure.

Limitations of Traditional Procurement BOMs

Traditional bills of materials track basic procurement part numbers and assembly logistics, but fail to record manufacturing origin, silicon provenance, or cryptographic component integrity. They cannot detect unauthorized hardware modifications or counterfeit chips.

The Hardware Bill of Materials (HBOM) Initiative

The HBOM initiative establishes standardized formats and tooling to track hardware component origins, silicon design provenance, and supply chain lineage from fabrication through final device assembly.

Empowering Risk-Informed Procurement

Adopting HBOMs enables government agencies and critical infrastructure operators to audit hardware supply chains, verify component integrity, and make informed risk decisions without relying solely on geographic trade restrictions.

talks.title: Hacking the Nautical Rules of the Road: Turn Left for Global Pwnage
talks.teaser: Explores how manipulating maritime rudder angle controllers to violate International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) causes severe disruption.
talks.summary:
COLREGs and Maritime Navigation Safety

The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) define universal navigation rules that mariners follow to ensure predictable vessel interactions and avoid collisions in congested waterways.

The Strategic Importance of 'Don't Turn to Port'

A fundamental guideline in maritime navigation is avoiding turns to port (left) in head-on or crossing situations. Under COLREG rules, turning to port directly violates established passing protocols and places full legal and operational liability on the vessel initiating the turn.

Cyber-Physical Manipulation of Rudder Controls

Manipulating cyber-physical systems—such as digital rudder angle controllers or NMEA-connected autopilots—can force an unexpected port turn. In maritime chokepoints and narrow channels, an induced port turn causes critical collision hazards with oncoming commercial traffic.

Legal Liability and Maritime Cyber Defense

Understanding the nautical rules of the road is crucial for maritime cybersecurity researchers and defenders to evaluate the true physical impact and legal liability resulting from compromised shipboard control systems.

talks.title: Full Disclosure, Full Color: Story of This Year's BBV Badge
talks.teaser: Takes a behind-the-scenes look at designing and manufacturing the Bug Bounty Village electronic badge, combining multi-layer PCBs and interactive CTF puzzles.
talks.summary:
Engineering Electronic Conference Badges

Creating custom electronic conference badges requires integrating artistic circuit board design, embedded firmware programming, and interactive puzzle engineering within strict manufacturing constraints.

PCB Art and Multi-Layer Fabrication

The Bug Bounty Village badge utilizes intricate silkscreen art, exposed copper planes, and specialized solder mask layering to create multi-color visual aesthetics alongside high-density LED matrix displays.

Embedded Hardware Architecture

The badge architecture incorporates low-power microcontrollers, interactive capacitive touch pads, and power management circuits designed to run for days on standard battery packs while powering dynamic visual effects.

Integrating CTF Puzzles and Firmware Challenges

Embedded into the badge firmware is a standalone Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge, allowing conference attendees to reverse engineer communication protocols and extract hidden puzzle flags directly from hardware interfaces.

talks.title: Real Exploits, Testbed Validation, Policy Gaps in Maritime Connectivity
talks.teaser: Presents vulnerability analysis and web interface exploits (CVE-2023-44852 to CVE-2023-44857) targeting maritime VSAT antenna control units and testbed validations.
talks.summary:
Vulnerabilities in Maritime Satellite Comms

Very Small Aperture Terminal (VSAT) satellite systems provide critical internet and telemetry links for maritime vessels and offshore platforms. Despite their vital role in vessel operations, VSAT modems and controllers frequently contain unpatched security vulnerabilities.

Re-Hosting and Analyzing VSAT Firmware

By extracting and re-hosting firmware from widely deployed antenna control units (ACUs), researchers identified multiple critical vulnerabilities across web management interfaces, cataloged as CVE-2023-44852 through CVE-2023-44857.

Remote Exploitation and Vessel Testbed Validation

Exploiting these ACU web interface flaws enables unauthenticated remote code execution and full modem takeover. Testing within experimental maritime testbeds demonstrated how attackers could disable vessel communications or manipulate antenna positioning.

Policy Gaps and Recommendations for Maritime Defense

Securing maritime satellite connectivity requires updating international maritime cybersecurity standards, enforcing secure firmware baselines, and implementing network segmentation between satellite modems and shipboard operational controls.

talks.title: They Deployed Health AI on Us: We’re Bringing the Rights & Red Teams
talks.teaser: Introduces the Patient AI Rights framework and a community-driven red teaming methodology to stress test clinical AI models and chatbots for bias and failure modes.
talks.summary:
Deployment of AI in Clinical Healthcare

Artificial intelligence models, diagnostic algorithms, and clinical chatbots are rapidly being deployed across healthcare environments. However, many systems enter clinical workflows without rigorous independent testing, patient consent, or comprehensive algorithmic auditing.

The Patient AI Rights Framework

The Patient AI Rights Initiative establishes a patient-authored ethical framework defining core rights regarding health data privacy, algorithmic transparency, and protection against automated clinical harm.

Community Red Teaming for Health AI

Applying offensive security testing methodologies to healthcare AI involves systematically evaluating models for failure modes, algorithmic bias, prompt injection vulnerabilities, and unauthorized data leakage from patient records.

Building an Open-Source Health AI Red Team Toolkit

Developing community-driven evaluation toolkits empowers security researchers, bioethicists, and patient advocates to audit clinical AI implementations and advocate for robust safety guardrails.

talks.title: Sometimes You Find Bugs, Sometimes Bugs Find You
talks.teaser: Chronicles serendipitous bug bounty discoveries, from unexpected blind XSS triggers to misdirected sensitive internal data distributions.
talks.summary:
The Unpredictable Nature of Bug Bounty Hunting

While bug bounty hunting is often structured around methodical asset enumeration and automated scanning, many high-severity vulnerabilities are discovered through serendipity, observation, and unexpected system interactions.

Unexpected Triggers and Blind XSS Payloads

Payloads injected months earlier into obscure application input fields frequently fire unexpectedly in internal back-office administrative portals, demonstrating how delayed execution paths uncover critical vulnerabilities.

Misdirected Communications and Internal Leakage

Configuration errors in email distribution lists and developer notification channels can mistakenly add external researchers to private internal feeds, exposing confidential customer records and internal credentials without active exploitation.

Cultivating Observational Awareness

Maximizing bug bounty success requires maintaining keen situational awareness, recognizing anomalous application responses, and investigating odd system behaviors beyond standard checklist testing.

talks.title: Resilient & Reconfigurable Maritime Comms
talks.teaser: Presents an SDN and SDR-driven cross-layer framework utilizing SATCOM infrastructure for resilient, reconfigurable communications across autonomous vessels.
talks.summary:
Communication Challenges in Autonomous Maritime Operations

The expansion of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), and connected commercial shipping relies on continuous data transfer across remote and dynamic ocean environments.

Cyber-Physical Vulnerabilities in Maritime Networks

Compromised IT systems aboard vessels provide direct pathways into Operational Technology (OT) networks, exposing propulsion and navigation systems to remote tampering when satellite links are disrupted.

Cross-Layer SDN and SDR Framework

An adaptive framework combining Software-Defined Networking (SDN) with Software-Defined Radios (SDR) enables vessels to dynamically reconfigure wireless frequencies, modulation schemes, and routing paths across SATCOM and mesh links in response to jamming or network degradation.

Resilience in Resource-Constrained Environments

Simulations demonstrate that cross-layer dynamic bandwidth allocation maintains mission-critical command links while ensuring cryptographic isolation between vessel telemetry and operational control traffic.

talks.title: Red Teaming Space: Hacking the Final Frontier
talks.teaser: Explores the emerging discipline of space red teaming, applying offensive testing methods to satellites, ground stations, and mission control infrastructure.
talks.summary:
Expanding Attack Surfaces in Space Systems

Commercialization and the rapid growth of satellite constellations have transformed space systems into prime targets for nation-state and cyber threat actors. Traditional security models frequently overlook the specialized architectures of spaceborne assets.

Principles of Space Red Teaming

Space red teaming adapts offensive security methodologies to test space vehicles, uplink/downlink communication paths, ground telemetry stations, and cloud-based mission control centers under realistic threat conditions.

Exploitation Vectors Across Space Segments

Attack vectors range from radio frequency signal hijacking and command injection on unauthenticated telemetry streams to exploiting web management consoles at satellite ground stations.

Building Threat-Informed Space Defenses

Establishing robust space defense requires integrating offensive testing into mission design phases, enforcing cryptographic validation on satellite command links, and hardening ground-based telemetry infrastructure.

talks.title: Fingerprinting Maritime NMEA2000 Networks
talks.teaser: Constructs a testbed NMEA 2000 CAN bus system to develop deterministic sensor fingerprints and detect anomalous traffic in maritime vessel networks.
talks.summary:
NMEA 2000 Protocol Architecture in Maritime OT

Modern commercial and recreational vessels rely on NMEA 2000 (built upon the ISO 11783 CAN bus standard and SAE J1939) to interconnect critical navigation instruments, GPS receivers, radar units, wind sensors, and multifunction displays.

Lack of Baselines in Maritime CAN Networks

Despite widespread adoption, understanding normal versus abnormal traffic patterns on NMEA 2000 networks is challenging due to the scarcity of open-source datasets and baseline behavioral models.

Developing Deterministic Sensor Fingerprints

Using a five-node hardware testbed, researchers captured baseline communication datasets across Parameter Group Numbers (PGNs) and derived deterministic timing and payload fingerprints for each sensor on the bus.

Validating Anomaly Detection Under Attack

Subjecting the testbed to message spoofing, fuzzing, and denial-of-service attacks demonstrated that deterministic fingerprints accurately identify rogue nodes and manipulated data frames in real time.

talks.title: Never Enough About Cameras: Firmware Keys Hidden Under the Rug
talks.teaser: Demonstrates remote code execution vulnerabilities in popular Dahua perimeter surveillance cameras discovered through firmware key extraction.
talks.summary:
In this technical reverse engineering session on the DEF CON 33 Creator Stage, a hardware security researcher explores firmware cryptographic flaws and vulnerability discovery in commercial IP cameras. Opening at 00:00, the presenter details the reverse engineering process required to inspect protected embedded device firmware images.

At 05:02, the speaker details cryptographic recovery techniques, demonstrating how tracing AES substitution boxes (S-boxes) and inspecting call hierarchies in disassemblers helps locate embedded decryption routines. At 10:00, the presentation uncovers flawed obfuscation schemes, highlighting hardcoded static keys and rudimentary byte-increment loops deployed by manufacturers in failed attempts to conceal encryption secrets.

Moving to vulnerability analysis at 15:01, the researcher dissects exposed device RPC functions and memory safety vulnerabilities in camera management daemons. Concluding at 20:02, the speaker demonstrates crafting return-oriented programming (ROP) gadget chains to achieve unauthenticated remote root execution, while reviewing the responsible disclosure and remediation timeline with the vendor. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Cryptocurrency Weekend Keynote
talks.teaser: Explains oblivious computation algorithms to hide access patterns in encrypted databases, with applications across blockchains, contact discovery, and AI.
talks.summary:
Information Leakage in Encrypted Databases

Traditional encrypted databases protect stored data contents at rest, but fail to hide access patterns. Observing which memory locations or records are queried reveals highly sensitive information in applications like private contact discovery, blockchain state access, and large language model inference.

Principles of Oblivious Computation

Oblivious computation algorithms, including Oblivious RAM (ORAM) and oblivious data structures, mathematically decouple observable physical memory accesses from logical user queries, guaranteeing provable privacy against observing adversaries.

Constructing Simple and Provably Secure Algorithms

Elaine Shi outlines efficient algorithmic constructions for oblivious computation that minimize bandwidth overhead and computational latency while providing rigorous cryptographic security proofs.

Real-World Applications in Signal and Ethereum

Oblivious computation is increasingly deployed in privacy-critical protocols, including Signal's private contact discovery service and emerging Ethereum scaling architectures, demonstrating practical feasibility at scale.

talks.title: Cryptocurrency Opening Keynote
talks.teaser: Introduces the DEF CON cryptocurrency track, covering emerging industry trends, upcoming workshops, the vendor area, and the Cryptocurrency Cyber Challenge.
talks.summary:
Welcome to the DEF CON Cryptocurrency Village

The DEF CON Cryptocurrency track brings together researchers, developers, and practitioners to explore decentralized technologies, cryptographic vulnerabilities, and emerging threats across the blockchain ecosystem.

Industry Trends and Academic Perspectives

Chad Calease and Param D Pithadia provide an overview of current shifts in cryptocurrency security, smart contract formal verification, decentralized finance exploits, and institutional adoption trends.

Workshops and Hardware Demonstrations

Conference attendees can participate in hands-on workshops covering blockchain forensics, hardware wallet security, zero-knowledge proofs, and decentralized application auditing.

The Cryptocurrency Cyber Challenge and Community Hub

Announcing the competing teams in the annual Cryptocurrency Cyber Challenge, the organizers highlight interactive CTF events and invite attendees to engage with speakers and vendors throughout the conference.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering Marine Engines: Make Powerboats Do Your Bidding
talks.teaser: Reverse engineers proprietary closed-source electronic engine controls and throttle protocols on modern outboard marine engines for autonomous navigation.
talks.summary:
The Expanding Autonomous Vessel Ecosystem

The market for autonomous surface vessels and uncrewed boats is expanding rapidly, with open-source autopilots like ArduPilot widely available. However, marine propulsion systems remain closed, proprietary black boxes.

Proprietary Engine Control Architecture

Unlike the automotive sector, marine outboard and inboard engine manufacturers tightly restrict interface control documents (ICDs) and utilize proprietary CAN and serial protocols for throttle, shifting, and steering actuation.

Reverse Engineering Outboard Protocols

Alex Lorman details the process of reverse engineering electronic engine control units across major marine manufacturers, analyzing CAN message timing, bus arbitration, and throttle position commands from jet-skis to high-horsepower outboard motors.

Bridging Open Autopilots to Marine Propulsion

Translating reverse-engineered CAN commands into open-source flight controller protocols enables seamless, autonomous throttle and steering control, paving the way for low-cost autonomous research vessels.

talks.title: Secure Code Is Critical Infrastructure: Hacking Policy for Public Good
talks.teaser: Advocates for treating secure software code as vital critical infrastructure, bridging application security practices with public policy reforms.
talks.summary:
A Canadian civic technologist and software security advocate argues that secure code and vulnerability disclosure frameworks must be treated as essential national critical infrastructure on the Creator Stage [00:11]. The speaker critiques sluggish government cybersecurity policies, pointing out systemic vulnerabilities such as public sector portals failing basic security baselines like mandatory HTTPS enforcement [05:19].

The presentation examines the operational shortcomings of government supply chain directives that mandate manual reviews of every software dependency, calling instead for automated, enforceable baseline security controls [10:04]. The speaker recounts systemic breaches across Canadian federal agencies—including incidents at the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) [14:55]—and chronicles grassroots advocacy efforts in Ottawa to establish legally protected vulnerability disclosure programs (VDPs) and direct public funding for critical open-source software maintenance [19:32, 24:20].

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: 10 Years of IoT Village: Insights in the World of IoT
talks.teaser: Reflects on a decade of IoT Village security research, vulnerability discoveries, and the evolution of connected device defense.
talks.summary:
A Decade of IoT Security Research

Since its founding at DEF CON, IoT Village has served as a central hub for embedded device security research, zero-day disclosures, and community education across thousands of connected products.

Evolution of Vulnerability Classes

Reflecting on ten years of research highlights how IoT vulnerabilities have transitioned from basic hardcoded credentials and unauthenticated telnet daemons to complex firmware encryption bypasses, supply chain flaws, and memory corruption exploits.

Impact on Vendor Practices and Regulations

Persistent public disclosures and responsible disclosure initiatives have spurred meaningful improvements in manufacturer security baselines, firmware signing practices, and international IoT cybersecurity labeling standards.

The Future of Connected Device Security

Looking ahead, IoT Village organizers discuss emerging challenges in consumer IoT, medical devices, and smart infrastructure, emphasizing the ongoing necessity of independent security research.

talks.title: How Computers Kill People: Marine Systems
talks.teaser: Analyzes cyber-physical safety risks in integrated bridge and propulsion controls aboard commercial maritime vessels where software bugs threaten lives.
talks.summary:
Cyber-Physical Safety in Marine Environments

Commercial maritime operations rely heavily on automated systems for navigation, engine management, ballast control, and dynamic positioning. When these software systems fail or are manipulated, the consequences pose direct threats to human life and vessel stability.

Architecture of Integrated Bridge Systems

Modern ship bridges integrate electronic chart display and information systems (ECDIS), autopilots, radar, and engine telegraphs over interconnected digital networks. Flaws in message parsing or sensor synchronization can cause loss of vessel control in hazardous waters.

Case Studies of Critical Marine System Failures

Michael DeVolld and Austin Reid analyze real-world marine incidents where sensor corruption, software deadlocks, or unintended control inputs led to groundings, collisions, and catastrophic propulsion loss.

Engineering Rigor and System Resiliency

Preventing cyber-physical marine disasters requires rigorous fail-safe engineering, physical manual overrides, isolated emergency steering systems, and comprehensive crew training in manual navigation.

talks.title: How AI + Hardware Can Transform Point of Care Workflows
talks.teaser: Presents a pocket-sized 10-watt bedside inference device running local 3B language models on a CM5 and RP2040 for private clinical workflows.
talks.summary:
Clinical Workflow Bottlenecks in Healthcare

Healthcare environments generate massive volumes of patient vital signs, medical imagery, and clinical notes. However, accessing and processing this data at the bedside is constrained by strict privacy regulations and unreliable hospital Wi-Fi networks.

Custom Embedded Hardware Architecture

PamirAI engineers developed a compact, 10-watt bedside inference device incorporating a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 (CM5), an RP2040 co-processor, and a sunlight-readable E-ink display tailored for clinical environments.

On-Device Local Inference

The device executes a 3-billion-parameter language model entirely on-device alongside local speech-to-text transcription models, providing private, low-latency AI reasoning without transmitting clinical data to cloud servers.

Offline Sensor Integration and MCP Hub

An embedded software hub interprets natural language instructions (such as 'log heart rate every five minutes') into automated sensor data collection routines, enabling rapid device deployment even during network outages.

talks.title: Operational Twilight: APTs, OT, & Geopolitics of a Dying Climate
talks.teaser: Examines how climate change impacts water and energy infrastructure and how advanced persistent threat groups exploit these stressed OT environments.
talks.summary:
Convergence of Climate Stress and Cyber Warfare

Climate change is placing unprecedented physical stress on global energy grids, municipal water distribution networks, and agricultural infrastructure. Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups strategically exploit these vulnerabilities during periods of extreme environmental stress.

Targeting Strained Critical Infrastructure

Nation-state actors recognize that physical infrastructure operating near capacity—such as power grids during severe heatwaves or water management systems during droughts—is exceptionally fragile and vulnerable to cascading disruptions from targeted cyberattacks.

Geopolitical Motivations and APT Tradecraft

Cybelle Oliveira examines the geopolitical motivations driving state-sponsored cyber operations against environmental critical infrastructure, analyzing TTPs used to penetrate OT networks and manipulate supervisory control data.

Defensive Resilience and Strategic Planning

Strengthening infrastructure resilience requires integrating physical climate risk models with cybersecurity threat intelligence, prioritizing fail-safe operations, and hardening critical control loops.

talks.title: Moonlight Defender: Purple Teaming in Space!
talks.teaser: Demonstrates purple team methodologies applied to satellite ground segments and flight software to validate threat detections and improve space cyber defenses.
talks.summary:
Applying Purple Teaming to Space Operations

As space infrastructure becomes increasingly critical for global navigation, communications, and defense, securing satellite architectures requires collaborative, iterative security testing between offensive operators and mission defenders.

Space Attack Surface and Emulation Scenarios

Ben Hawkins details purple teaming exercises targeting satellite ground segment networks, mission command servers, and simulated onboard flight software payloads, emulating realistic adversary techniques.

Validating Telemetry and Anomaly Detections

Executing controlled offensive maneuvers allows space defenders to evaluate whether satellite telemetry pipelines, ground station logs, and ground control monitoring systems correctly identify anomalous command sequences in real time.

Lessons Learned and Operational Hardening

Purple team exercises in space systems reveal critical visibility gaps, enabling mission teams to refine intrusion detection rules, implement cryptographic command verification, and harden ground-to-space communications.

talks.title: Fear vs Physics: Diagnosing Grid Chaos
talks.teaser: Separates cyberattacks from physical power dynamics, analyzing grid oscillations, transformer fires, and blackstart scenarios to diagnose grid disturbances.
talks.summary:
Misconceptions Surrounding Electric Grid Failures

When major power grid disruptions occur, media and analysts frequently rush to suspect malicious cyberattacks. However, the majority of grid disturbances originate from physical power dynamics, equipment physics, and control system interactions.

Low-Frequency Oscillations in Bulk Power Systems

As renewable generation and inverter-based resources expand, low-frequency oscillations increasingly emerge across transmission networks. These oscillations stem from control system tuning and physical network conditions rather than adversarial cyber intrusions.

Analyzing Historical Incidents: Blackouts and Equipment Fires

Emma Stewart dissects real-world power events, including the Iberian Peninsula blackout and the London transformer fire, demonstrating how protection relays acted correctly to preserve equipment and how operational blackstart plans functioned under stress.

Replacing Fear with Engineering Facts

Accurately securing power infrastructure requires deep domain knowledge of power system physics, robust telemetry analysis, and distinguishing physical operational phenomena from genuine cyber threats.

talks.title: What is Dead May Never Die: The Immortality of SDK Bugs
talks.teaser: Explores how unpatched software development kits from major chipset vendors perpetuate persistent vulnerabilities across millions of consumer IoT devices.
talks.summary:
The Ubiquity of Vendor Chipset SDKs

Chipset manufacturers provide Software Development Kits (SDKs) containing reference drivers, pre-compiled binaries, and web management services to help device vendors quickly bring smart hardware to market.

Flaws Frozen in Upstream Codebases

When vulnerabilities exist within reference SDK code, those flaws are bundled into dozens of commercial product lines across multiple vendors. Once hardware is deployed in the field, upstream SDK patches rarely propagate down to end-user devices.

Botnet Exploitation of Zombie SDK Vulnerabilities

Richard Lawshae demonstrates old-day and zero-day vulnerabilities in major chipset SDKs that have been continuously exploited by IoT botnet operators across millions of connected cameras, routers, and smart plugs.

Cleaning the Zombie SDK Ecosystem

Mitigating systemic SDK vulnerabilities requires chipset vendors to adopt transparent patch management, device manufacturers to maintain active firmware update pipelines, and automated SBOM tracking across embedded software.

talks.title: Navigating the Invisible
talks.teaser: Demonstrates low-cost OSINT techniques leveraging vessel tracking, port data, and open intelligence to detect anomalous behavior and maritime security risks.
talks.summary:
Open-Source Intelligence in the Maritime Domain

The vastness of the maritime domain conceals significant operational and cybersecurity risks. Leveraging publicly accessible open-source intelligence (OSINT) allows defenders to build comprehensive threat intelligence pictures without expensive proprietary tooling.

Analyzing Vessel Tracking and AIS Data

Monitoring Automatic Identification System (AIS) broadcasts, vessel registry databases, and port departure logs enables analysts to detect anomalous vessel movements, spoofed location reports, and suspicious offshore rendezvous.

Integrating Port Logistics and Social Media Telemetry

Correlating maritime shipping manifests, satellite imagery, and port worker social media data surfaces hidden supply chain bottlenecks, physical security vulnerabilities, and potential smuggling operations.

Actionable Intelligence for Sector Defenders

Practitioners can implement low-cost data collection workflows and automated alert pipelines to maintain proactive situational awareness across critical maritime shipping lanes.

talks.title: Hull Integrity: Applying MOSAICS to Naval Mission Systems
talks.teaser: Breaks down how the US Department of Defense MOSAICS Block 1 framework provides real-time OT monitoring and behavioral threat detection on Naval vessels.
talks.summary:
Cyber-Physical Attack Surfaces in Naval Fleets

Modern naval vessels integrate interconnected operational technology (OT) systems managing propulsion, electrical power distribution, damage control, and weapons systems, creating complex cyber-physical attack surfaces.

The MOSAICS Block 1 Framework

Developed by the Department of Defense, the More Situational Awareness for Industrial Control Systems (MOSAICS) Block 1 framework establishes reference architectures for real-time asset discovery, monitoring, and behavioral threat detection tailored for mission-critical ICS.

Adapting Reference Architectures to Shipboard Systems

Michael Frank explains how the Department of the Navy adapts MOSAICS to legacy and modern naval systems, overcoming severe constraints regarding compute availability, network bandwidth, and disconnected maritime operations.

Operationalizing OT Defense at Scale

Deploying automated behavioral detection and safe asset inventory aboard naval vessels enhances fleet cyber survivability without interfering with critical mission operations or weapons control.

talks.title: HoloConnect AI: From Space to Biohacking
talks.teaser: Introduces HoloConnect AI, an air-gapped holographic agent running local offline AI models developed for space missions and surgical assistance.
talks.summary:
Air-Gapped Holographic Intelligence

Originally developed and tested aboard the International Space Station (ISS), HoloConnect AI combines holographic display hardware with local, offline artificial intelligence models for environments where cloud connectivity is impossible.

Expanding from Aerospace to Medical Devices

Deploying offline holographic AI agents in healthcare settings enables surgeons and clinicians to interact with voice- and vision-aware AI assistants during complex surgical procedures without risking clinical data exposure.

Secure Embedded Stacks and Voice Spoofing Defense

Operating AI agents on air-gapped embedded hardware requires sandboxed model execution, secure local sensor processing, and acoustic anti-spoofing controls to prevent unauthorized voice actuation.

Live Demonstrations and Future Horizons

Demonstrating medical-grade holographic agents running without external network connectivity highlights how edge AI can deliver instant, private decision support in high-stakes environments.

talks.title: How AI + Hardware can Transforming Point-of-Care Workflows
talks.teaser: Demonstrates custom CM5 and RP2040 embedded hardware paired with local speech and language models for automated offline clinical data logging.
talks.summary:
Bedside Clinical Computing Challenges

Clinical environments produce continuous streams of patient telemetry, diagnostic imaging, and physician notes. However, strict healthcare privacy rules and network instability complicate cloud-based AI assistance at the bedside.

Hardware Architecture: CM5, RP2040, and E-Ink

PamirAI engineers created a dedicated bedside device combining a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, an RP2040 microcontroller, and an ultra-low-power E-ink display to run local inference within a tight 10-watt power envelope.

Software Layer and MCP Hub Integration

The embedded software stack features an MCP Hub that translates natural language clinician requests into automated sensor logging and structured record updates without requiring external network connectivity.

Rapid Sensor Integration via Local AI

Leveraging on-device AI models enables rapid integration and calibration of medical telemetry sensors, empowering clinicians with immediate, automated documentation right at the point of care.

talks.title: Firmware Decryption: For, and By, the Cryptographically Illiterate
talks.teaser: Breaks down practical software and hardware techniques for decrypting obfuscated and encrypted IoT firmware without requiring advanced cryptography math.
talks.summary:
The Rise of Encrypted IoT Firmware

Device manufacturers increasingly encrypt and obfuscate firmware update images to thwart reverse engineering and security audits. However, the cryptographic implementations in embedded devices often contain fundamental flaws.

Locating Keys in Hardware and Bootloaders

Craig Heffner demonstrates how security researchers can extract decryption keys from physical flash chips, unencrypted bootloader stages (such as U-Boot), and hardware debug interfaces (JTAG/UART) without advanced mathematical cryptanalysis.

Analyzing Flawed Symmetric Key Implementations

Many vendors rely on static, shared AES keys hardcoded across entire product families or employ flawed XOR and substitution ciphers. Reverse engineering previous unencrypted firmware revisions frequently reveals the decryption routines.

Practical Tooling and Unpacking Workflows

Equipped with practical scripts and firmware analysis frameworks, researchers can successfully unpack encrypted vendor updates and inspect embedded binaries for vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Your Passkey is Weak: Phishing the Unphishable
talks.teaser: Demonstrates an effective phishing attack vector against synced passkeys and outlines operational safeguards for enterprise passkey deployments.
talks.summary:
The Promise and Reality of Passkeys

FIDO2 passkeys are widely promoted as the definitive solution to phishing, leveraging public-key cryptography and origin-bound credentials to prevent credential harvesting attacks.

Phishing Vectors Against Synced Passkeys

Chad Spensky demonstrates a practical attack chain targeting consumer-synced passkey ecosystems. By manipulating device enrollment flows and user trust assumptions, attackers can induce users into delegating access or pairing unauthorized synchronization devices.

Social Engineering and Device Pairing Exploits

Attacking the passkey ecosystem shifts the adversary focus from password harvesting to credential syncing mechanisms, QR-code authentication flows, and account recovery handoffs.

Recommendations for Secure Passkey Implementation

Enterprises adopting passkeys must configure strict device attestation policies, mandate hardware security keys for high-privilege roles, and educate users on verifying cross-device pairing prompts.

talks.title: Bare Metal Reverse Engineering
talks.teaser: Presents a structured Ghidra methodology for reverse engineering stripped ARM Cortex bare-metal and FreeRTOS embedded binaries using SVD and BSim plugins.
talks.summary:
Challenges of Bare-Metal Firmware Analysis

Reverse engineering stripped bare-metal firmware and RTOS binaries on ARM Cortex platforms is notoriously difficult due to the absence of symbol tables, dynamic loaders, and standard file formats.

Mapping Board Support Packages via SVD Loader

Using the SVD (System View Description) loader plugin in Ghidra, analysts map memory-mapped hardware peripheral registers directly to MCU hardware specifications, instantly contextualizing hardware control routines.

Deconstructing the Hardware Abstraction Layer

Custom type recovery scripts and function pattern matching allow researchers to identify hardware initialization sequences, peripheral clock gating, and GPIO driver logic without source code.

RTOS Kernel Reconstruction with BSim

Applying Ghidra’s BSim plugin facilitates signature matching against FreeRTOS and other embedded kernels, recovering task creation routines, scheduler priorities, and inter-process communication constructs in complex firmware.

talks.title: Dead Reckoning: Hijacking Marine Autopilots
talks.teaser: Discloses an unauthenticated firmware update vulnerability in marine autopilots, allowing arbitrary CAN injection via NMEA 2000 chart plotters.
talks.summary:
Vulnerabilities in Marine Navigation Computers

Autopilot systems aboard commercial and recreational vessels translate navigation course data into physical rudder actuations over NMEA 2000 CAN networks, operating as critical cyber-physical bridges.

Unauthenticated Firmware Update Flaws

Carson Green and Rik Chatterjee demonstrate how a popular marine autopilot computer accepts unsigned firmware update files (.swup) via SD card slots or networked chart plotters without cryptographic validation or hardware authentication.

Persistent Code Execution and CAN Injection

Crafting a malicious update package allows attackers to gain persistent firmware-level execution on the autopilot hardware, enabling arbitrary CAN packet injection, course spoofing, and remote rudder disruption across the vessel's NMEA 2000 bus.

Remediation for Marine Control Systems

Mitigating marine firmware hijacking requires enforcing cryptographic signature verification in bootloaders, disabling unauthenticated network update mechanisms, and implementing CAN bus intrusion detection.

talks.title: Prompt Scan Exploit AI’s Journey Through 0Days and 1000 Bugs
talks.teaser: Chronicles the deployment of XBOW, an autonomous AI offensive agent that discovered over 200 open-source vulnerabilities and submitted 1,000 bug bounty reports.
talks.summary:
Autonomous AI in Offensive Security

The development of autonomous AI agents capable of end-to-end vulnerability research represents a major milestone in automated security testing.

Architecture of the XBOW Offensive Agent

XBOW integrates large language models with specialized dynamic analysis environments, code scanners, and exploit generators, autonomously exploring web and software attack surfaces without human intervention.

Real-World Vulnerability Discoveries and Impact

Deploying XBOW against real-world targets resulted in the discovery of over 200 security flaws across open-source projects and the submission of more than 1,000 bug bounty reports, earning top rankings on major bounty platforms.

Implications for the Future of Vulnerability Research

The success of autonomous AI agents highlights the accelerating pace of vulnerability discovery, necessitating automated defensive remediation pipelines and AI-driven patch generation.

talks.title: Referral Beware, Your Rewards Are Mine
talks.teaser: Uncovers client-side gadgets, race conditions, and business logic flaws hidden within referral and reward systems across major bug bounty programs.
talks.summary:
The Overlooked Attack Surface of Referral Systems

Referral and reward programs are ubiquitous in consumer web applications but are frequently viewed by bug bounty hunters as routine functionality with minimal security impact.

Business Logic and Race Condition Vulnerabilities

Whit Taylor demonstrates how concurrent API requests and flawed database state transactions allow attackers to exploit race conditions, claiming unlimited referral credits and bypassing payout limits.

Client-Side Gadgets and Exploit Chaining

Improperly sanitized referral parameters introduce client-side path traversal and cookie-injection gadgets that can be chained with other client-side flaws to execute account takeovers.

Securing Reward and Referral Architectures

Defending promotional and referral workflows requires enforcing strict database row locking, validating referral token state idempotently, and sanitizing all client-side redirect parameters.

talks.title: VDP in Aviation: How it Shouldn't be Done!
